title.text: Laoag Cathedral and the Sinking Bell Tower

title_en.text: Laoag Cathedral and the Sinking Bell Tower

tagline.text: An Italian Renaissance-style facade and a brick bell tower that sinks year by year

location.label: Location
location.text: Central Laoag City, Ilocos Norte (A. Bonifacio Street)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱0–500 (local transport and snacks; no admission fee)

children.text: Laoag Cathedral (Saint William's Cathedral) is the most eye-catching building in Laoag, the main city of Ilocos Norte, and right beside it stands a brick bell tower said to sink a little each year. It sits in the middle of town and is easy to see on foot, which makes it a good first stop on a Laoag itinerary.

The official name is Saint William's Cathedral. It stands in Laoag City, the provincial capital of Ilocos Norte, and is the main church of the Diocese of Laoag. According to Wikipedia, when the Augustinians founded the parish here in 1580 the church was a small building of wood and thatch. The present church is said to have had its foundations laid in 1612; after a fire in 1843 it was restored between 1873 and 1880. It became a cathedral in 1961 when the Diocese of Laoag was created. Revolutionaries occupied the church in 1898 and American forces in 1899, and the Aglipayans and the Roman Catholic Church then contested ownership, which the Catholics regained. The facade was renewed with lime plaster in 1936, and there was further renovation in 1971–1972. Having been repaired many times through fire, war and earthquakes, it is not a church built all at once, and keeping that in mind makes a visit more interesting.

The style is described as Italian Renaissance. The two-storey facade has an arched entrance with two pairs of columns on each side, and a recessed niche near the top holds an image of the patron saint, San Guillermo el Ermitaño (Saint William the Hermit). The windows are made of capiz shell with wrought-iron screens, and inside there is a main altar with smaller altars on either side. Unlike many other old Philippine churches, the facade decoration is restrained and clearly symmetrical, so photographs come out well balanced.

Within walking distance of the cathedral, the "sinking bell tower" is the best-known sight in the area. This brick tower, which survived in an earthquake-prone region, is presumed to have been built after the 1707 earthquake. It is about
(about 147 feet) tall and stands about
from the main church. Because it rests on sandy ground, it is said to sink about
2.5 cm

(1 inch) a year. The sinking is described as even rather than a tilt, and there is said to be no immediate danger of collapse, though some say it could eventually be buried in the ground. Only authorized people may enter the tower, so visitors see it from the outside.

Laoag is a coastal city on the South China Sea with a population of about 110,000 according to a visitor guide. The airport is described as having flights to Manila, Cebu, Calayan Island and Basco in Batanes, and the city has sights such as the market and a large "LAOAG" welcome sign. This guide is for travelers spending half a day in central Laoag. Seeing the cathedral and tower takes an hour or two, so it combines well on foot with Laoag's other sights (the museum, the provincial capitol and Aurora Park), and with an extra day you can visit Sarrat Church, Paoay Church and the La Paz Sand Dunes. I could not confirm official Mass or opening times, so check locally before you go.

blocks.title: The facade of Saint William's Cathedral

children.text: The two-storey facade, the two pairs of columns, the arched entrance and the image of Saint William in the niche above are typical of the Italian Renaissance style. The facade was renewed with lime plaster in 1936. It looks best from across the street, where the whole facade fits in one view.
The brick tower, about
tall, is said to sink about
2.5 cm

a year. It features four massive corner columns and a winding stairway inside, and it once had a large clock on its west face. One account says the bricks were bonded with molasses, sablot leaf juice, lime and sand.
The tower has survived several minor earthquakes, which is why scholars cite it as an example of "Earthquake Baroque." The cathedral also suffered only slight damage in the 1983 Luzon earthquake.
The cathedral's windows are made of capiz shell and fitted with wrought-iron screens.
Inside are a main altar and two smaller side altars, with an image of Saint William on the lower level of the main altar. Please be quiet during Mass.

The area around the cathedral and tower is the center of Laoag. Laoag is the main city of Ilocos Norte, and heritage from Spanish colonial buildings, Baroque churches and Marcos-era mansions remains in and around town. From here you can walk toward the market, the plaza and the museum, and the city also has Aurora Park and the Ilocos Norte Provincial Capitol.
Photos of the tower easily pick up the road and traffic around it, so early morning, when the road is quiet, gives a cleaner shot. Take photos from the sidewalk for safety.

items.title: Half a day downtown
items.subtitle: The cathedral, the tower and a walk through Laoag

children.text: Walk from your hotel in central Laoag to Saint William's Cathedral. It is quieter to go in after the morning Mass is over.
Look around the facade and the altars inside.
Go to the bell tower, photograph it from all sides and look at the ground and bricks up close.
Visit the city museum (Museo Ilocos Norte) or Aurora Park.
Have lunch at a downtown restaurant serving Ilocano food.
Entry to the tower is limited to authorized people, so do not try to go in; view it from outside.
See the cathedral and the bell tower.
Take a jeepney or tricycle to see the exterior of Sarrat Church.
Return to Laoag for lunch.
Go to Paoay Church and look around its buttresses.
Watch the late afternoon light at the La Paz Sand Dunes.
Sarrat Church may have restricted access because of the 2024 earthquake damage.

There are flights from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO). Wikipedia describes it as the busiest commercial airport in the Ilocos region. Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
From the airport, go into the city by tricycle or taxi. Check the fare locally.
Routes change often, so check airline announcements before departure.
Buses from Manila to Laoag are run by companies such as GV Florida, Viron Transit, Maria de Leon, Partas and Fariñas Transit. The trip takes about
10–12 hours
. Check fares locally.
According to Wikipedia, the road distance from Manila to Laoag is about
487 km
(via the southern route).
Laoag has taxis, jeepneys, tricycles and kalesas (horse-drawn carriages). The cathedral and tower are close together and can be reached on foot.
Minibuses and jeepneys to nearby towns (Pagudpud, Batac, Vigan, Carmen and others) also leave from the city.

Laoag has a tropical savanna climate, with a dry season from November to April and a wet season from May to October. According to the Wikipedia climate table, January is the coolest month, with a mean daily minimum of about
, and the mean daily maximum in April and May is about
. August is the wettest month, with about 594 mm of rain.

The city is said to be affected by four to five tropical cyclones (typhoons) a year, so leave spare days in the rainy season. For walking, early mornings and late afternoons in the dry season are the most comfortable.

Laoag is the lodging base for Ilocos Norte. Hotels and guesthouses cluster downtown, and Wikipedia describes the Fort Ilocandia Resort on the edge of the city as the only five-star hotel in the north. To see the cathedral and tower on foot, it is best to stay downtown. From Laoag you can also make day trips by jeepney and minibus to Vigan (in Ilocos Sur) or to Pagudpud in the far north, so one hotel can serve as a base.
In Ilocos Norte, empanada (a fried rice-dough pastry) and longganisa (Ilocano-style sausage) are often recommended. They are easy to find in the city market and on the street; check prices locally.
When going inside the cathedral, dress modestly, covering shoulders and knees.
Refrain from taking photos or speaking loudly inside during Mass. Check the Mass schedule locally.
The cathedral may be closed. Some reviewers found it locked when no Mass was scheduled, so come back at a different time.
Visit the tower in daylight. It takes only 5–10 minutes, so combine it with other stops.
It is hot with little shade by day, so bring a hat and water.
In crowded markets, carry your belongings in front of you.
Museo Ilocos Norte is in the same city, and visiting it together with the cathedral helps you understand Ilocos history.
Carry cash (pesos). Many small shops and markets do not accept cards.
I could not confirm opening hours or Mass times for the cathedral and tower. Only authorized people may enter the tower, so do not go into off-limits areas.
Opening hours and fees can change, so check the latest announcements. This guide is based on Wikipedia, travel blogs and the Ilocos Norte tourism office.
Sources disagree on when the cathedral was built, giving 1580, 1590, 1612, 1880 and so on. This guide follows Wikipedia's account of foundations in 1612 and completion of restoration in 1880.
The rate at which the tower sinks is given as about 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) depending on the source, and is not an exact measurement. Treat it as a rough figure.
Watch out for motorcycles and tricycles when crossing roads.
Roads in town can flood during typhoons and the rainy season, so check weather information.
